t.1.2.1: The good is one thing and the pleasant quite another; these two, with differing aims, bind a man. Of the two, it goes well for him who takes up the good, but he who chooses the pleasant falls away from his goal.
t.1.2.2: The good and the pleasant both approach a man; the wise one, having examined them closely, tells them apart. The wise one chooses the good over the pleasant, while the dull one chooses the pleasant for the sake of gaining and keeping.
t.1.2.3: You, Naciketas, having reflected on desires that are dear and dear in form, have cast them aside; you have not taken up this chain made of wealth, in which many mortals sink.
t.1.2.4: Far apart and opposed, leading in different directions, are these two: what is known as ignorance and what is known as knowledge. I regard Naciketas as one who longs for knowledge, for the many desires did not tempt you.
t.1.2.6: The passage to the hereafter does not shine forth to the childish one, heedless and deluded by the delusion of wealth. Thinking, "This world exists, there is no other," he falls again and again into my power.
t.1.2.5: Dwelling in the midst of ignorance, wise in their own eyes and thinking themselves learned, the deluded stagger aimlessly round and round, like the blind led by one who is himself blind.
t.1.2.7: He who is not to be obtained by many even for hearing, whom many, even while hearing, do not know: wondrous is the one who speaks of him, skilful the one who attains him, wondrous the one who knows him when taught by the skilful.
t.1.2.8: This, when taught by an inferior man, is not easily understood, though it be pondered in many ways. Unless it is taught by another, there is no access to it here, for it is subtler than the subtlest measure and beyond the reach of reasoning.
t.1.2.9: This understanding is not to be gained by reasoning; only when taught by another does it lead to true knowledge, dearest one. You have attained it, for you are steadfast in truth indeed! May we always find a questioner like you, Naciketas.
t.1.2.10: I know that treasure is impermanent, for that which is permanent is not attained through things that are not permanent. Therefore the Nāciketa fire was built by me with impermanent materials, and I have attained the permanent.
t.1.2.11: Having seen the attainment of desire, the foundation of the world, the endlessness of sacrifice, the farther shore of fearlessness, the great praise, the wide-ranging foundation, you, Naciketas, being wise, have with steadfastness let it all go.
t.1.2.12: Having known through the attainment of inner yoga that God, hard to see, hidden, deeply entered within, set in the secret cave, dwelling in the abyss, the ancient one, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow.
t.1.2.14: That which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, other than what has been and what is yet to be, tell me that.
t.1.2.13: Having heard this and fully grasped it, a mortal who has drawn out the righteous one and attained this subtle one rejoices, for he has obtained what is worthy of rejoicing. I deem the abode wide open for Naciketas.
t.1.2.15: The goal which all the Vedas declare, which all austerities proclaim, and desiring which people live the life of brahmacarya, that goal I tell you briefly.
t.1.2.17: This syllable, indeed, is Brahman; this syllable, indeed, is the supreme. Having known this very syllable, whoever desires anything, that is his.
t.1.2.18: This support is the best, this support is the highest; having known this support, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
t.1.2.19: The wise one is neither born nor does he die; he has not come from anywhere, nor has he become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain.
t.1.2.21: Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is set in the secret cave of this creature. One who is free from desire and beyond sorrow beholds that majesty of the Self through the tranquility of the senses.
t.1.2.20: If the slayer thinks that he slays, and if the slain thinks that he is slain, both of them do not understand: this one neither slays nor is slain.
t.1.2.22: Though sitting, he travels far; though lying down, he goes everywhere. Who but me is able to know that god who rejoices and does not rejoice?
t.1.2.23: Having known the Self as bodiless within bodies, stable amid the unstable, great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.
t.1.2.24: This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. He whom this Self chooses, by him alone is it to be attained; to him this Self reveals its own form.
t.1.2.25: Not one who has not turned away from wrongdoing, not one who is not at peace, not one who is not composed, nor even one whose mind is not tranquil, could attain him through insight.
t.1.2.26: He for whom both the brahman and the kṣatra become food, and for whom death is the sauce poured over it, who knows thus where he is?
